title: LagLLM: LLM-empowered lead–lag dependency learning for spatial-temporal time series forecasting
claim: A staged system combines data-driven and knowledge-driven structure learning, then feeds the resulting structure into a fine-tuned model for prediction.
layout: 4 panels: top end-to-end pipeline, three zoomed module panels below, left-to-right
description: A gray header strip labeled (a) Framework shows a left-to-right chain of white boxes with arrows. Historical inputs and spatial structure go to a Spatial-Temporal Tokenizer, then a Hybrid Lead-Lag Graph Construction Module, a Structural Token Sorting Module, a Fine-Tuning LLM with a LoRA badge, an Output Projection Module, and finally Predicted Outputs. Below are three zoomed panels. (b) shows the tokenizer: stacked time-series windows are patchified, clustered with the spatial graph, and grouped into patches. (c) is the largest panel. A blue Data-Driven Modeling box with learnable embeddings, adaptive graph construction and an initial graph sits above a Knowledge-Driven Reasoning box. That box has structural pooling and a spatial mask, plus a frozen LLM that reads a prompt and produces a semantic mask. All branches merge in a yellow Combine block into a lead-lag graph of three colored groups. (d) shows colored token sequences passing through message passing and a Sort step, bottom to top. Yellow operation boxes and blue arrows draw the eye.
caption: Overview of LagLLM.
abstract: Spatial-temporal time series forecasting is challenging due to complex lead-lag dependencies, which are often ignored or inadequately modeled by existing methods. Thus, we propose LagLLM, the first LLM-empowered framework that explicitly models lead–lag dependencies by unifying data-driven dynamics modeling and knowledge-driven semantic reasoning. Specifically, LagLLM constructs a lead-lag graph by integrating learnable embeddings, spatial proximity, and prompt-guided reasoning from a frozen LLM, which can capture lead-lag dependencies informed by the underlying data structure and semantic knowledge. In addition, LagLLM introduces structural token sorting based on the graph, which can make a fine-tuned LLM explicitly perceive directional and delayed interactions. Experiments on eight real-world datasets show that LagLLM achieves the state-of-the-art performance with improved accuracy, robustness, and interpretability. The code is available at https://github.com/w2obin/LagLLM-2026.
